splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether the actuary may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond what was specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: No tolling
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because the statute does not authorize such tolling, and the term expires as originally set regardless of the supervisee's compliance.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the stricter gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law. The outcome determines whether federal prisoners face a more restrictive regime than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to state voting and ballot-counting rules. The outcome could fundamentally reshape how courts evaluate candidate standing to challenge election administration practices, with implications for mail-in voting deadlines and other election procedures nationwide.

positions.label: Standing exists
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws before an election takes place based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: No standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge state ballot-counting rules pre-election because they cannot demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury traceable to the challenged law.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when construing ambiguous provisions that carry criminal penalties, such as Sentencing Guidelines enhancements.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps agency deference in criminal sentencing contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has taken on additional significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions with criminal consequences, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference to Sentencing Commission commentary) takes precedence over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt offenses within the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson, or whether it impermissibly expands the guideline text. The split has deepened after Kisor v. Wilkie narrowed the scope of deference to agency interpretations of their own rules.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative and includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) under Stinson and Kisor, and that conspiracy qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 cannot add them and is not entitled to deference, especially after Kisor narrowed deference principles.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in § 3553(f)(1). The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that defendants are disqualified only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. The split creates sentencing disparities based solely on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance at issue to be federally scheduled. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits have applied a federal-match requirement. The split affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: No federal-match requirement
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes any offense under state law, even if the particular substance is not controlled under federal law.

positions.label: Federal-match required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under federal law, applying a categorical approach that requires a federal analogue.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can serve as a basis for compassionate release. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold that such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permit consideration of such changes. This affects prisoners serving lengthy sentences under since-amended mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission's contrary policy statement exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement at § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for the breach of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the original offense and the defendant's history.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits have held that revocation sanctions should be based on the seriousness of the violation conduct and the defendant's characteristics, rather than as punishment for the breach itself. This affects hundreds of supervised release revocations annually.

positions.label: May punish for the breach
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences as punishment for violations of supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Revocation is not punishment for the breach
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation is to sanction the defendant's breach of trust, not to punish the violation conduct itself, and courts should focus on the original offense and defendant's history.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody (such as First Step Act time credits) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may use a civil rights action such as Bivens.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions that affect release timing must be brought as habeas petitions or may proceed as civil actions. The Eighth Circuit has acknowledged this unresolved conflict that has persisted for over half a century, affecting federal prisoners' access to judicial review of BOP decisions regarding First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the fact or duration of confinement, including First Step Act time-credit disputes, must be brought via habeas corpus and cannot proceed as civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge conditions of confinement or certain BOP decisions through civil rights actions (§ 1983 or Bivens) even when habeas may also be available, as long as the challenge is not solely to the fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is treated as a civil matter (with a 60-day appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (with a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split on this question.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises from a criminal case and therefore the criminal appeal deadline governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value occurring between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate, while other courts have reached the opposite conclusion based on the structure and legislative history of § 348(f). The split affects debtors' incentives to convert and the distribution to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, based on the statute's structure, legislative history, and the policy of encouraging good-faith conversions from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order that would be 'effectively unreviewable' after final judgment.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have applied a more restrictive approach to the collateral order doctrine for sealing motions. The split affects litigants' ability to protect sensitive medical information during ongoing litigation.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that warrants immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the interest can be vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
